What: Families tuned for different workloads. General purpose: E2 (cost-optimised), N2/N2D/N4 (balanced), C4A/T2A (Arm). Compute-optimised: C3/C4, H3. Memory-optimised: M3/M4 (SAP HANA, huge in-memory DBs). Accelerator-optimised: A3/A4 (NVIDIA H100/H200/B200), G2 (L4 GPUs). Storage-optimised: Z3. Custom machine types let you pick exact vCPU and memory (E2/N-series).

column1: Explain: Persistent Disk, Hyperdisk and Local SSD
column2: What: Block storage for VMs. Persistent Disk (pd-standard, pd-balanced, pd-ssd) is durable, network-attached, zonal or regional (synchronously replicated across two zones for HA). Hyperdisk is the newer generation, with performance (IOPS and throughput) provisioned separately from capacity. Local SSD is physically attached, very fast, and ephemeral: the data is lost when the VM stops or is deleted.

column1: Explain: Images, snapshots, machine images and instance templates
column2:
What: Image: a bootable disk template (public images, or your own "golden" hardened images, often built with Packer). Snapshot: an incremental, point-in-time backup of a disk, stored regionally or multi-regionally, and schedulable. Machine image: a whole VM (config + all disks) for cloning or backup. Instance template: an immutable VM configuration used by MIGs.

GCP: Banks typically maintain hardened golden images (CIS benchmarks), restrict which images can be used with the org policy compute.trustedImageProjects, and use snapshot schedules for backups.

What: A fleet of identical VMs created from an instance template and managed as one.

How: Autoscaling (on CPU, load-balancer serving capacity, Cloud Monitoring metrics, or schedules), autohealing (recreates VMs that fail an application health check), rolling updates and canaries (max surge / max unavailable), regional MIGs (spread across zones for HA), stateful MIGs (keep disks and IPs for stateful apps).

GCP: The VM equivalent of a Kubernetes Deployment. It's the backbone of lift-and-shift HA designs behind load balancers.

What: Spare capacity at a large discount (often 60–91% off) that Google can reclaim at any time, with a 30-second warning. No minimum or maximum runtime. (Preemptible VMs were the older version, limited to 24 hours.)

GCP: Good for fault-tolerant batch work, CI runners, stateless GKE node pools, rendering, and some ML training with checkpointing. Never for databases or anything that can't tolerate sudden loss.

What: GPUs (NVIDIA L4, A100, H100/H200, B200…) are general accelerators for ML training and inference, graphics and simulation. TPUs are Google's custom ML accelerators (v5e, v5p, v6e Trillium and newer), very efficient for large-scale training and serving, especially with JAX or TensorFlow and increasingly PyTorch.

How: Attached to VMs, GKE node pools, Cloud Run (GPUs), and the AI platform's training and prediction. Capacity is scarce: use reservations, Dynamic Workload Scheduler (queue for capacity, flex-start) or committed use.

What: A process (or a few) isolated using kernel features: namespaces (its own view of processes, network and filesystem) and cgroups (CPU and memory limits), packaged with everything it needs to run. They share the host kernel, so they're lighter and start faster than VMs, but isolation is weaker.

How: Build once, run anywhere: the same image runs on a laptop, Cloud Run, GKE or another cloud, which is why containers count as a portability and exit-strategy lever.

GCP: Cloud Run adds a gVisor sandbox (gen1) or a microVM (gen2 execution environment) for stronger isolation. GKE Sandbox (gVisor) is available for untrusted workloads.

What: An image is a stack of read-only layers plus metadata (entrypoint, env), following the OCI standard. It's referenced by tag (:v1.2, mutable) or digest (@sha256:…, immutable).

GCP: Artifact Registry stores container images and language packages (Maven, npm, Python, Go, apt/yum), regional or multi-regional, with IAM, vulnerability scanning, cleanup policies, and remote/virtual repositories (proxy and cache public registries such as Docker Hub and PyPI, important for controlled egress in banks).

What: An open-source system for running containers across a cluster of machines, using declarative desired state and continuous reconciliation.

How: Control plane: the API server (everything goes through it), etcd (the state store), the scheduler (places Pods on nodes), controllers (loops that drive actual state towards desired state). Nodes: the kubelet (runs Pods), a container runtime (containerd), kube-proxy or eBPF (Service networking). You kubectl apply YAML manifests and controllers make it so.

GCP: GKE runs the control plane for you (and, in Autopilot, the nodes too).

What: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing a network namespace (one IP) and volumes, scheduled together. A ReplicaSet keeps N identical Pods running. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to give declarative rolling updates and rollbacks.

What: A stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of Pods (selected by labels).

How: Types: ClusterIP (internal only, the default), NodePort (a port on every node), LoadBalancer (provisions a cloud load balancer; on GKE an L4 passthrough NLB, internal or external), Headless (no virtual IP; DNS returns the Pod IPs, used with StatefulSets).

GCP: For HTTP(S), use Gateway API or Ingress on top of Services, which provisions Application Load Balancers with container-native NEGs.

What: Kubernetes APIs for L7 routing into the cluster. Ingress is the older, limited API. Gateway API is the newer, role-oriented one: *GatewayClass* (infrastructure provider), *Gateway* (owned by the platform team), *HTTPRoute* (owned by app teams), with traffic splitting, header matching and cross-namespace routing.

GCP: The GKE Gateway controller provisions global or regional, external or internal Application Load Balancers from Gateway resources. It supports multi-cluster Gateways for multi-region.

column1: Explain: StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs
column2: What: StatefulSet: Pods with stable identities (db-0, db-1) and their own persistent volumes, for databases and quorum systems. DaemonSet: one Pod per node (log agents, security agents). Job: run to completion. CronJob: scheduled Jobs.

What: ConfigMaps inject non-secret configuration. Secrets inject sensitive values, but they're only base64-encoded, and stored in etcd (encrypted at rest on GKE, with optional application-layer encryption using Cloud KMS).

GCP: Prefer Secret Manager, accessed through Workload Identity or the Secret Manager CSI driver / add-on, so secrets have central IAM, audit and rotation.

column1: Explain: Namespaces, resource requests and limits
column2:
What: Namespaces divide a cluster for teams or environments (scoping RBAC, quotas and network policies). Requests are what a Pod is guaranteed and scheduled on. Limits are the maximum it may use (exceeding the memory limit gets the container OOM-killed; CPU is throttled).

GCP: GKE Autopilot bills by Pod requests, so right-sizing requests is cost control.

column1: Explain: Autoscaling: HPA, VPA, cluster autoscaler
column2: What: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): changes the replica count based on CPU, memory or custom/external metrics (for example Pub/Sub backlog). Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA): recommends or sets requests. Cluster autoscaler / node auto-provisioning: adds or removes nodes when Pods can't be scheduled or nodes sit idle.

column1: Explain: Probes: liveness, readiness and startup
column2: What: Readiness: is the Pod ready for traffic? (Failing removes it from Service endpoints.) Liveness: is it stuck? (Failing restarts the container.) Startup: give slow starters time before liveness checks begin.

What: Autopilot: Google manages the nodes, scaling, security hardening and upgrades. You deploy Pods and pay for their requested resources. This is the default recommendation. Standard: you manage node pools (machine types, GPUs, autoscaling, upgrades) and pay per node.

How: Both have a Google-managed control plane with an SLA. Both support regional clusters (control plane and nodes across 3 zones), release channels (Rapid, Regular, Stable, Extended) and maintenance windows and exclusions.

GCP: Choose Standard when you need node-level control: specific GPUs or TPUs, special kernels, privileged DaemonSets, or bin-packing tuned for cost.

What: An infrastructure layer for service-to-service traffic. A proxy (usually Envoy) sits beside each workload as a sidecar, or as a node-level or ambient proxy, and handles mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and authorization policies, and produces uniform telemetry, without code changes. Istio is the main open-source mesh.

GCP: Cloud Service Mesh (managed Istio / Traffic Director) for GKE, VMs and Cloud Run. It gives automatic workload identity certificates, SLO-ready golden-signal metrics, and authorization policies like "only payments-api may call ledger-api".

What: Helm: a package manager for Kubernetes (templated "charts"). Kustomize: template-free overlays per environment. Fleets (GKE Enterprise): manage many clusters as one: Config Sync (GitOps), Policy Controller (OPA Gatekeeper constraints), multi-cluster ingress or gateway, and Cloud Service Mesh.

What: Fully managed, request-driven containers. Give it an image (or source), and it serves HTTPS with autoscaling, including to zero.

How: Key concepts: revisions (immutable code + config) and traffic splitting across them with tags; concurrency (requests per instance, default 80, up to 1000); min/max instances; CPU allocation (request-based, or instance-based "always on"); request timeout up to 60 minutes; startup CPU boost; gen2 execution environment (full Linux compatibility, network file systems); multi-container sidecars; volume mounts (Cloud Storage FUSE, NFS, in-memory, secrets); GPUs; ingress settings (all / internal / internal + load balancer); IAM authentication (roles/run.invoker); Direct VPC egress; HTTP/2 and gRPC, WebSockets and server-sent events; service identity (its service account); regional deployment (use a load balancer for multi-region).

GCP: The default runtime for APIs, web apps, AI agents and backends-for-frontends. Common in bank GenAI stacks for orchestrators, tools and MCP servers.

column1: Explain: Cloud Run jobs and worker pools
column2: What: Jobs: containers that run to completion, with parallel tasks (each gets an index), retries, and up to days of runtime. Used for batch, ETL, migrations and scheduled work through Cloud Scheduler. Worker pools: always-on, non-HTTP background workers (for example pulling from Pub/Sub or Kafka).

What: Functions-as-a-service (formerly Cloud Functions, now built on Cloud Run). Write a function, and it's triggered by HTTP or by events (Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, Firestore, audit-log events through Eventarc).

GCP: Good for small glue code. Anything bigger or longer-lived fits better as a Cloud Run service.

What: Extra latency when a new instance has to start (pull the image, start the runtime, run initialization) before serving a request. It happens when scaling from zero or during sharp scale-out.

How: Mitigations: min instances (always-warm capacity, which you pay for), smaller images, lazy initialization, startup CPU boost, language and runtime choice (Go is faster than JVM without tuning), and connection reuse.
What: How many requests one instance handles at the same time. A higher setting means fewer instances and lower cost, but the code must be thread-safe or async and stay within per-instance memory.

What: No servers to provision or manage, automatic scaling (often to zero), and paying for use rather than capacity.

GCP: Compute (Cloud Run, functions), data (BigQuery, Firestore, Spanner with autoscaling), messaging (Pub/Sub, Eventarc), orchestration (Workflows), AI (Gemini APIs).

What: Horizontal scaling adds or removes instances: needs stateless design, a load balancer, and has effectively no ceiling. Vertical scaling gives an instance more CPU and RAM: simple, limited by the largest machine, and often needs a restart.

How: Autoscalers act on signals (CPU, requests, queue depth, custom metrics), with cooldowns or stabilization to avoid flapping. Predictive autoscaling uses history.

What: A stateless service keeps no client state between requests (state lives in a DB, cache or token), so any instance can serve any request, and scaling and failover are trivial. A stateful service keeps state locally (sessions in memory, local files, a database engine), which makes scaling, failover and deployment harder.

What: Principles for cloud-native apps: config in the environment, backing services as attached resources, stateless processes, port binding, disposability (fast start, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM), dev/prod parity, logs as event streams to stdout, and more.

GCP: Cloud Run, GKE and Cloud Logging assume these principles.
What: Google's original PaaS (standard environment: sandboxed runtimes; flexible environment: containers on VMs). It still runs many legacy apps, but Cloud Run is the recommended choice for new work.
What: A managed batch scheduler that provisions VMs (including Spot and GPUs) to run containerized or script jobs at scale, then tears them down. Used for HPC, risk simulations and large data jobs.

column1: Explain: Google Cloud VMware Engine and Bare Metal Solution
column2: What: VMware Engine: a dedicated VMware SDDC (vSphere, vSAN, NSX) running in Google Cloud, so VMware estates can be lifted without re-platforming. Bare Metal Solution: dedicated physical servers near Google regions for workloads like Oracle RAC that can't be virtualized or need special licensing.

column1: Explain: Developer environments (Cloud Shell, Cloud Workstations)
column2: What: Cloud Shell: a free, ephemeral browser terminal with tools pre-installed. Cloud Workstations: managed, policy-controlled dev environments running inside your VPC, which banks like because source code never sits on laptops and egress is controlled.

column1: Explain: VM Manager and patch management
column2: What: OS inventory, patch compliance reporting, scheduled patch jobs, and OS policies (config management) across VM fleets, through the OS Config agent.

column1: Explain: Block vs file vs object storage
column2: What: Block: raw volumes the OS formats and mounts (one VM, low latency, used for databases and boot disks): Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk. File: a shared hierarchical filesystem over NFS or SMB (many clients, POSIX semantics): Filestore, NetApp Volumes. Object: whole immutable objects in a flat namespace, accessed over HTTP APIs, with practically unlimited scale and cheap storage: Cloud Storage.

What: Object storage with very high durability (designed for 11 nines). Buckets (globally unique names, with a location and default class) hold objects (immutable blobs with metadata).

How: Strong global consistency for reads after writes, overwrites, deletes and listings. Locations: regional, dual-region (with optional turbo replication, an RPO of 15 minutes), multi-region. Access: uniform bucket-level access (IAM only, recommended) or legacy ACLs, public access prevention, signed URLs. Protection: object versioning, soft delete (deleted objects recoverable for a set number of days), retention policies and bucket lock (WORM; it satisfies some record-keeping rules), object holds. Movement: Storage Transfer Service, gcloud storage, parallel composite uploads. Data lake integrations through BigLake.

GCP: The landing zone for data lakes, model artifacts, RAG source documents, backups, logs archives and static sites.

What: Standard (hot, no minimum), Nearline (30-day minimum, about monthly access), Coldline (90-day minimum), Archive (365-day minimum). All have millisecond first-byte latency and the same API and durability. Colder classes cost less to store but more to retrieve, and have early-deletion charges.

How: Autoclass moves objects between classes automatically based on access. A bucket's class is a default. Each object has its own class.

What: Bucket rules that change storage class or delete objects based on conditions: age, created-before date, number of newer versions, live or noncurrent state, prefix or suffix.

GCP: For example: move logs to Coldline after 30 days, delete after 7 years. Delete noncurrent versions after 90 days. Lifecycle can't delete objects under a retention policy before it expires.

column1: Explain: Signed URLs and signed policy documents
column2:
What: Time-limited URLs that grant whoever holds them access to one object (GET to download, PUT to upload) without an IAM identity. Signed with a service account key or, keylessly, through the IAM signBlob API.

GCP: The standard pattern for browser and mobile uploads straight to Cloud Storage, which keeps large files out of your API servers.

What: Managed NFS file shares (Filestore tiers: Basic, Zonal, Regional, Enterprise). NetApp Volumes adds SMB and NetApp features. Used for lift-and-shift apps needing a shared POSIX filesystem, GKE ReadWriteMany volumes, and some ML training data.

What: Durability: the probability your data isn't *lost* (for example 11 nines). Availability: the proportion of time you can *access* it (for example 99.95%). Data can be perfectly durable and temporarily unavailable.

What: OLTP (online transaction processing): many small, concurrent reads and writes of individual records, with low latency and strict consistency. Bank ledgers, payments, customer profiles. OLAP (online analytical processing): fewer, huge queries scanning and aggregating millions or billions of rows. Reporting, risk, ML features.

GCP: OLTP: Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Spanner, Firestore, Bigtable (key lookups). OLAP: BigQuery. HTAP (both) features: AlloyDB's columnar engine, Spanner Data Boost, BigQuery federated queries to Spanner and Cloud SQL.

What: Row stores keep each record's fields together, so fetching or updating one record is fast (OLTP). Columnar stores keep each column together, so scanning a few columns over many rows is fast, and the data compresses very well (OLAP).

What: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold before and after), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work), Durability (committed means it survives crashes).

GCP: Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and Spanner are fully ACID (Spanner even across regions). Firestore has ACID transactions over documents. Bigtable gives single-row atomicity only. BigQuery supports multi-statement transactions but isn't built for OLTP.

What: How strongly concurrent transactions are separated. Read committed (the default in PostgreSQL) prevents dirty reads, but non-repeatable reads and phantoms can happen. Repeatable read / snapshot isolation: a stable snapshot, but *write skew* is possible. Serializable: as if transactions ran one after another (the safest, with more conflicts and retries).

GCP: Spanner defaults to serializable (with strict "external consistency"). For money movement, know which level you're running at, and handle retries on conflicts.

What: What readers are guaranteed to see after a write. Strong / linearizable: every read sees the latest committed write. Eventual: replicas converge over time, so a read may be stale. In between: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, bounded staleness.

GCP: Strong: Cloud Storage, Spanner, Firestore, Cloud SQL primary, and Bigtable within a single cluster. Eventual: Cloud SQL read replicas, Bigtable cross-cluster replication, caches. Spanner offers stale reads (bounded or exact staleness) for lower latency when slightly old data is fine.

What: CAP: during a network Partition, a distributed system must choose Consistency (reject or block some requests) or Availability (answer, possibly with stale data). PACELC extends it: Else (normally), choose between Latency and Consistency.

GCP: Spanner chooses consistency, and gets very high availability by running on Google's redundant private network and TrueTime. Bigtable multi-cluster and caches choose availability and latency.

What: Keeping copies of data on multiple nodes or locations. Synchronous: a write is acknowledged only when the replicas have it, so RPO = 0, but write latency includes the slowest replica (fine within a region, painful across distant regions). Asynchronous: acknowledge first, replicate later, so writes are fast, but RPO > 0 (recent writes can be lost on failover) and replicas lag.

How: Leader/follower (single writer, many readers), multi-leader (conflict resolution needed), consensus (Paxos/Raft) (a majority quorum agrees, as in Spanner).

GCP: Cloud SQL HA uses synchronous replication to a standby in another zone. Read replicas and cross-region replicas are async. Spanner uses Paxos-based synchronous replication across zones or regions. Regional Persistent Disk replicates synchronously across 2 zones.

What: Splitting data across nodes by key so that storage and throughput scale horizontally. Range sharding (contiguous key ranges) or hash sharding.

How: A good key spreads load evenly. Hotspots happen when keys are sequential (timestamps, auto-increment IDs), because all new writes hit one shard.

GCP: Spanner and Bigtable split data by key range automatically. Avoid monotonically increasing leading keys: use UUIDv4, bit-reversed sequences, or a hashed or salted prefix. BigQuery "partitioning" is a related but different idea: it splits tables (usually by date) to prune scans.

What: Data structures (B-trees mostly, plus hash, GIN, vector indexes) that make lookups by a column fast, at the cost of write overhead and storage.

GCP: Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and Spanner have secondary indexes. Firestore needs an index for every query (single-field indexes are automatic, composite ones you define). Bigtable has only the row key, so design your key around your queries. Vector indexes: ScaNN (AlloyDB), HNSW/IVF (pgvector), Vector Search.

column1: Explain: Normalization, denormalization and star schemas
column2:
What: Normalization: split data into related tables to avoid duplication and update anomalies (OLTP). Denormalization: duplicate data or nest it to avoid joins (analytics, NoSQL). A star schema has central *fact* tables (events, transactions) joined to *dimension* tables (customer, product, date).

GCP: BigQuery handles star schemas well, and it also rewards nested and repeated fields (STRUCT/ARRAY), which store child records inside the parent row to avoid joins.

What: Managed MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server. Google handles provisioning, patching, backups, replication and failover.

How: HA configuration: a primary plus a standby in another zone of the same region, with synchronous storage-level replication and automatic failover (about a minute). Read replicas (async, same or cross-region) can be promoted for DR. Automated backups + point-in-time recovery (PITR, from transaction logs). Private IP (through PSA or PSC) and the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy / language connectors (IAM-authorized, TLS, no allow-listing IPs). IAM database authentication. Maintenance windows. Editions: Enterprise and Enterprise Plus (better performance, near-zero-downtime maintenance, 99.99% SLA, larger data cache). It scales vertically, with storage up to tens of TB.

GCP: The default for "a normal relational app database" and lift-and-shift of MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQL Server.

What: A PostgreSQL-compatible database built by Google with compute separated from a distributed, log-based storage layer.

How: Faster transactional throughput than standard PostgreSQL, a columnar engine for fast analytics on live data, read pools for scaling reads, a 99.99% SLA, cross-region secondary clusters for DR, and AlloyDB AI: pgvector with ScaNN indexes, in-database calls to embedding and Gemini models, natural-language-to-SQL. AlloyDB Omni runs it anywhere (on-prem, other clouds).

GCP: Strong choice for demanding PostgreSQL workloads and for RAG, where you want vectors, metadata filters and transactional data in one place.

What: A globally distributed relational database with horizontal scale, strong external consistency and up to 99.999% availability (multi-region configurations; 99.99% regional).

How: Data is split by primary-key ranges across servers, and each split is replicated with Paxos across zones or regions. TrueTime (GPS- and atomic-clock-backed time with bounded uncertainty) gives globally ordered commit timestamps. It offers GoogleSQL or a PostgreSQL interface, interleaved tables (child rows stored with the parent), change streams, Data Boost (analytics without hurting OLTP), graph and vector search, full-text search. Capacity is measured in nodes or processing units, with autoscaling and editions.

What: Google's clock API that returns a time *interval* guaranteed to contain true time, using GPS and atomic clocks in each data centre. Spanner waits out the uncertainty at commit ("commit wait") so timestamps reflect real-time order everywhere.

What: A serverless, autoscaling document database. Collections contain documents (JSON-like, nested), which can contain subcollections.

How: Strongly consistent reads and queries, ACID transactions, real-time listeners (clients get pushed updates), offline SDKs for mobile and web, security rules for direct client access, TTL policies, PITR, and regional or multi-region locations (99.999% multi-region SLA). Two modes: Native (the full feature set) and Datastore mode (server-side, for the legacy Datastore API). Firestore also offers MongoDB compatibility and vector search.

What: A wide-column NoSQL store for massive throughput and single-digit millisecond latency at TB–PB scale. It's the technology behind Search, Maps and Analytics.

How: Each row has one row key, and the table is sorted by it. Columns are grouped into column families. Cells are versioned by timestamp. It offers single-row transactions only, no secondary indexes (beyond limited new features) and an HBase-compatible API. Clusters are made of nodes (throughput scales roughly linearly). Replication across clusters and regions is *eventually consistent*, with app profiles that route to one cluster or many.

GCP: Used for time series, IoT, market tick data, fraud feature lookups, personalization and ad-tech. Row key design (for example customerId#reverseTimestamp) is the whole game.

What: Managed in-memory data stores: Redis (and Redis Cluster), Valkey (the open-source Redis fork) and Memcached. Sub-millisecond latency.

How: Uses: caching, session state, rate-limit counters, leaderboards (sorted sets), pub/sub, queues, LLM response or semantic caches, vector search. HA with replicas and automatic failover. Private connectivity (PSC). Persistence (RDB/AOF) is optional. It's still memory first, so not a system of record.

What: Cache-aside (lazy loading): the app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the DB and fills the cache. Read-through: the cache loads from the DB itself. Write-through: write to the cache and DB together. Write-behind: write to the cache, flush to the DB later (risk of loss). Entries leave through TTLs and eviction (LRU, LFU).

How: Two hard problems: invalidation (when the source changes) and stampedes (thundering herd, when many misses hit the DB at once; fixed by request coalescing, jittered TTLs, early refresh).

GCP: Memorystore (application cache), Cloud CDN (edge), BigQuery result cache and BI Engine, LLM context caching (cache long prompts on the model side) and semantic caching (reuse answers to similar questions, through Apigee or a vector cache).

What: A serverless, petabyte-scale data warehouse with separate storage and compute and standard SQL. It's also the hub of GCP analytics and AI.

How: Storage: columnar (Capacitor format) on Colossus, organized as project → dataset (location-bound, the main access boundary) → tables and views. Compute: the Dremel query engine allocates slots (units of compute). Pricing: on-demand (per TB scanned) or capacity (editions with reservations and autoscaling slots). Ingestion: free batch loads, the Storage Write API (streaming, exactly-once), Pub/Sub BigQuery subscriptions, Datastream (CDC), Data Transfer Service. Features: partitioning and clustering, materialized views, BI Engine (in-memory acceleration), search indexes, vector search, BigQuery ML (train or call models, including Gemini, in SQL), remote functions (call Cloud Run from SQL), time travel (7 days) and fail-safe, authorized views and datasets, row-level security, column-level security with policy tags (and dynamic data masking), Analytics Hub (data sharing), BigLake / external tables (query GCS data in Iceberg or Parquet), multi-statement transactions.

What: Partitioning splits a table into segments by a date or timestamp column, ingestion time, or integer range. Queries that filter on the partition column only scan the matching partitions. Clustering sorts the data within partitions by up to 4 columns, so filters and aggregations on those columns read fewer blocks.

GCP: You can require a partition filter (require_partition_filter) to stop accidental full scans. Partition expiry is a way to implement retention policies.

column1: Explain: BigQuery slots, editions and reservations
column2: What: A slot is a virtual CPU for queries. On-demand pricing uses a shared pool with a per-project cap. Editions (Standard, Enterprise, Enterprise Plus) let you buy slot capacity with autoscaling and optional commitments. Reservations and assignments dedicate capacity to projects or folders (workload isolation: prod ETL separated from ad-hoc analysts).

column1: Explain: Data lake, data warehouse and lakehouse
column2:
What: Data lake: cheap object storage holding raw data in any format (schema-on-read). Warehouse: curated, structured, governed tables optimized for SQL (schema-on-write). Lakehouse: warehouse-style governance, transactions and performance on open table formats (Apache Iceberg, Delta, Hudi) in object storage, readable by many engines (BigQuery, Spark, Trino).

GCP: BigLake gives unified, fine-grained governance over GCS data and BigQuery, including BigLake Iceberg tables and a metastore. Common layering: raw/bronze → cleaned/silver → curated/gold.

What: GCP's data governance layer: a catalog (search and metadata across BigQuery, GCS, databases and AI assets), business glossary, data lineage (column-level lineage across BigQuery, Dataflow, Composer and others), data quality scans and data profiling, and lake/zone management with security policies.

GCP: It answers the regulator's questions "where did this number come from?" (lineage, as in BCBS 239 risk-data aggregation) and "who owns this dataset and what's in it?".

column1: Explain: Backup, PITR and Backup and DR Service
column2:
What: Backups are copies taken at intervals. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) replays transaction logs to restore to any second within a window. Backup and DR Service is GCP's centralized backup management (VMs, databases, file systems, GKE) with backup vaults that are immutable and indelible (protection against ransomware and insiders).

GCP: Cloud SQL (automated backups + PITR), AlloyDB (continuous backup + PITR), Spanner (backups + PITR up to 7 days), Firestore (PITR + scheduled backups), BigQuery (time travel + snapshots), GKE (Backup for GKE).
What: A fleet-wide dashboard for all your GCP databases (inventory, health, security and configuration issues, recommendations), with AI-assisted insights.

What: Batch processes a bounded dataset on a schedule (nightly risk runs, end-of-day reconciliations): simpler, cheaper, with higher latency. Streaming processes an unbounded flow of events continuously, with seconds of latency (fraud detection, real-time dashboards, alerts): harder, because of ordering, late data and state.

GCP: Batch: BigQuery SQL, Dataflow batch, Dataproc, Cloud Run jobs, Batch. Streaming: Pub/Sub or Kafka → Dataflow → BigQuery or Bigtable, or BigQuery continuous queries.

What: ETL: extract → transform (in a separate engine) → load the cleaned result. ELT: extract → load raw data into the warehouse → transform there with SQL. ELT has become the default with powerful warehouses like BigQuery.

GCP: ELT with BigQuery + Dataform (version-controlled SQL pipelines) or dbt. ETL with Dataflow, Dataproc or Data Fusion when you need heavy transformation, streaming, or data shaping before it lands (for example PII tokenization before the data reaches the lake).

What: Capturing row-level inserts, updates and deletes from a database's transaction log and streaming them elsewhere, without heavy queries on the source.

GCP: Datastream (serverless CDC from MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server and AlloyDB into BigQuery or Cloud Storage), Spanner change streams, Debezium on Kafka. A very common bank pattern: core systems on-prem → CDC → BigQuery for analytics and ML features.

column1: Explain: Queue vs pub/sub vs event log (stream)
column2:
What: Queue: each message goes to *one* consumer from a pool (work distribution), and is deleted once processed. Pub/sub: each message is copied to *every subscription* (fan-out), and each subscription is a queue for its consumers. Event log / stream (Kafka-style): an ordered, retained, append-only log split into partitions. Consumers track their own offset and can replay from any point.

GCP: Pub/Sub is pub/sub with per-subscription queues, plus retention and seek for replay. Managed Service for Apache Kafka is the log model. Cloud Tasks is a queue of HTTP calls to one target.

What: A global, serverless, autoscaling messaging service. Publishers send to topics, and subscriptions deliver to subscribers.

How: Subscription types: pull (StreamingPull for high throughput), push (HTTPS POST to an endpoint, for example Cloud Run, with OIDC authentication), BigQuery (writes straight into a table), Cloud Storage (batches into files). Delivery: messages are redelivered until acked, within an ack deadline that can be extended. Other features: retention (7 days by default, longer configurable; topic retention allows replay), seek (replay to a timestamp or snapshot), ordering keys (in order per key, within a region), exactly-once delivery (pull, per region), dead-letter topics, filtering (by attributes), schemas (Avro or Protobuf), message storage policy (restrict which regions store messages, which matters for UK residency), single message transforms, CMEK. Throughput scales automatically.

column1: Explain: Delivery semantics (at-most / at-least / exactly once)
column2:
What: At-most-once: may lose messages, never duplicates. At-least-once: never loses, may duplicate. This is the norm. Exactly-once: each message has its effect exactly once, which in practice means at-least-once delivery + deduplication or idempotent processing.

GCP: Pub/Sub is at-least-once by default, with an exactly-once option for pull subscriptions. Dataflow gives exactly-once *processing* inside the pipeline. BigQuery Storage Write API gives exactly-once writes with offsets.

What: Guaranteeing consumers see related messages in the order they were published.

How: Global ordering doesn't scale, so systems order per key: Pub/Sub ordering keys, Kafka partitions. A failure (an unacked message) blocks later messages for that key until it's resolved.

column1: Explain: Dead-letter topics and poison messages
column2:
What: A poison message fails processing every time (bad format, a bug) and would block or loop forever. A dead-letter topic (DLT/DLQ) receives messages after N failed delivery attempts, so the rest keep flowing, and someone can inspect or replay them later.

GCP: Pub/Sub subscriptions take --dead-letter-topic and --max-delivery-attempts. The Pub/Sub service agent needs publisher and subscriber roles for this. Alert on DLT backlog.

column1: Explain: Apache Kafka and Managed Service for Apache Kafka
column2:
What: Kafka is the open-source distributed event-log platform: topics split into partitions (ordered, replicated), producers, consumer groups (each partition is consumed by one member of the group), offsets, retention by time or size, a connector ecosystem (Kafka Connect) and stream processing (Kafka Streams).

GCP: Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka runs Kafka clusters for you. Choose it when you have Kafka skills, Kafka-native tools (Debezium, Connect) or multicloud portability needs. Choose Pub/Sub for serverless simplicity and native GCP integration.

What: Apache Beam is a unified programming model (Java, Python, Go, SQL, YAML) for batch *and* streaming pipelines. Dataflow is Google's serverless runner for Beam.

How: Pipelines are graphs of PCollections (datasets) and transforms (ParDo, GroupByKey, Combine, windowing). Dataflow handles autoscaling workers, Streaming Engine, dynamic work rebalancing, exactly-once processing, templates (Classic or Flex, for reusable launches), Dataflow Prime, and GPUs for ML inference in pipelines. Common sources and sinks: Pub/Sub, Kafka, GCS, BigQuery, Bigtable, Spanner, JDBC.

GCP: The standard engine for streaming ETL, real-time feature computation (fraud), and large batch transforms. Enrichment and ML inference (RunInference) can run inside the pipeline.

column1: Explain: Windowing, watermarks and late data
column2: What: Ways to aggregate an unbounded stream. Windows group events by event time: fixed / tumbling (every 5 minutes), sliding (5-minute windows every minute), session (bursts separated by gaps). A watermark is the system's estimate of "we've probably seen all events up to time T". Triggers decide when to emit results (at the watermark, early speculative results, late updates). Allowed lateness controls how long late events can still update a window.

What: Managed Apache Spark and Hadoop ecosystem (Hive, Presto/Trino, Flink). Clusters start in about 90 seconds. Dataproc Serverless runs Spark batches and interactive sessions without clusters.

How: Best practice: ephemeral, job-scoped clusters, with data in Cloud Storage (not HDFS) and metadata in a shared metastore. Use autoscaling and Spot secondary workers.

GCP: Choose it to migrate existing Spark or Hadoop jobs, or for Spark skills and libraries. Choose Dataflow for new serverless pipelines, especially streaming.

What: Managed Apache Airflow for orchestrating data pipelines as DAGs (directed acyclic graphs) of tasks, with operators for BigQuery, Dataflow, Dataproc, GCS, external systems, retries, SLAs, backfills and scheduling.

What: Develops, version-controls (git), tests and schedules SQL transformation pipelines in BigQuery (SQLX files with dependencies, assertions for data quality, incremental tables). Comparable to dbt, and native to BigQuery.
What: A visual, low-code ETL/ELT designer (based on open-source CDAP) with many connectors. Pipelines run on Dataproc. Suits teams that prefer GUI-built integrations.

column1: Explain: Data transfer and ingestion services
column2: What: Storage Transfer Service: bulk and scheduled transfers into GCS from other clouds, HTTP sources, on-prem file systems (through agents) or between buckets. Transfer Appliance: a physical device shipped to you for offline transfer of hundreds of TB to PB. BigQuery Data Transfer Service: scheduled loads from SaaS (Google Ads, Salesforce and others), other warehouses (Teradata, Redshift migrations) and GCS. gcloud storage: command-line copies.

What: Looker: an enterprise BI platform with a governed semantic layer (LookML defines metrics once), embedded analytics and APIs. Looker Studio: free, self-service dashboards and reports with many connectors.

GCP: Banks prefer Looker, because consistent, governed metric definitions matter for regulatory reporting. The semantic layer also grounds natural-language-to-data agents ("conversational analytics").

column1: Explain: BigQuery continuous queries and real-time analytics
column2: What: Continuous queries run SQL on data as it streams into BigQuery and export results continuously to Pub/Sub, Bigtable or other tables (for example real-time alerting with SQL only). Together with Storage Write API ingestion, BigQuery can handle near-real-time use cases without Dataflow.

column1: Explain: Data mesh and federated governance
column2:
What: An organizational approach where domain teams own their data as products (with SLAs, documentation and quality), on a self-service platform, under federated computational governance (global standards enforced automatically).

GCP: Often built with domain-owned projects and datasets, Dataplex for catalog and governance, Analytics Hub for sharing, and BigLake for shared lake storage.

What: Checks that data is complete, valid, unique, timely and consistent. In pipelines: schema enforcement, assertions (Dataform), Dataplex data-quality scans, Great Expectations-style tests, and quarantining bad records rather than failing everything.

What: Synchronous: the caller sends a request and waits for the response (REST, gRPC). It's simple and immediate, but it couples availability (if B is down, A fails) and latency (A's latency includes B's). Asynchronous: the caller hands off a message or event and continues (Pub/Sub, Kafka, Cloud Tasks). It decouples availability and buffers load, at the cost of eventual consistency, harder debugging and more complex error handling.

How: Rule of thumb: synchronous for queries and anything the user is waiting on. Asynchronous for side effects, fan-out, long-running work and integration between domains.

What: Request/response: "do this for me and tell me the result" (a command). Event-driven: services publish events ("PaymentSettled") describing facts that happened, and interested services react independently. Producers don't know who the consumers are.

How: Event types: notification (thin: an ID, so consumers call back for details), event-carried state transfer (fat: includes the data), domain events.

GCP: Pub/Sub, Eventarc (with the CloudEvents format), Kafka. For example, a "transaction posted" event fans out to fraud scoring, notifications, the ledger analytics feed and an agent that categorizes the spend.

What: An architectural style for HTTP APIs: resources identified by URLs (/accounts/123/transactions), manipulated with standard methods, stateless requests, representations (usually JSON), and meaningful status codes.

How: GET reads, POST creates (or triggers an action), PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes. Collections support filtering, sorting and pagination. Versioning goes in the path (/v1/) or headers.

GCP: Almost every Google API is available as REST (and gRPC). Google's API Improvement Proposals (AIPs) are a good REST design guide (resource names, standard methods, long-running operations, pagination).

column1: Explain: HTTP methods: safety and idempotency
column2: What: Safe methods don't change state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Idempotent methods have the same effect whether called once or many times: GET, PUT, DELETE (plus HEAD, OPTIONS). POST is not idempotent and PATCH isn't guaranteed to be.

What: 2xx success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 202 Accepted (async processing started), 204 No Content. 3xx redirect: 301/308 permanent, 302/307 temporary, 304 Not Modified. 4xx client error: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (actually *unauthenticated*), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 412 Precondition Failed (etag mismatch), 429 Too Many Requests (rate limited; respect Retry-After). 5xx server error: 500 Internal, 502 Bad Gateway (a proxy got a bad response from upstream), 503 Service Unavailable (overloaded or down; retryable), 504 Gateway Timeout (upstream too slow).

What: gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework. Services and messages are defined in Protocol Buffers (.proto), a compact binary serialization format with strong schemas, and client and server code is generated from them. It runs over HTTP/2.

How: Four call types: unary (request → response), server streaming (request → stream of responses), client streaming, bidirectional streaming. Built-in deadlines (propagated across hops), cancellation, metadata (headers), status codes, and backward-compatible schema evolution (field numbers; never reuse them).

GCP: Many Google APIs are gRPC-native (Pub/Sub, Spanner, Bigtable clients). Cloud Run supports gRPC, including streaming, with HTTP/2 end-to-end. Application Load Balancers and service mesh route gRPC. gRPC-Web or transcoding (API Gateway, Cloud Endpoints, Envoy) exposes gRPC services as REST/JSON to browsers.

What: A query language for APIs. Clients ask for exactly the fields they need from a typed schema in one request, which avoids over- and under-fetching across many REST calls. It has one endpoint, and mutations for writes and subscriptions for push.

What: A full-duplex, long-lived connection over a single TCP connection, started with an HTTP Upgrade handshake. Either side can send messages at any time.

GCP: Supported on Cloud Run (bounded by the request timeout, up to 60 minutes; clients must reconnect), GKE and Application Load Balancers (backend service timeout). Scaling needs care: connections pin to instances, so use session affinity and shared state through Memorystore pub/sub or similar. Live trading UIs, chat, real-time voice agents (for example the Gemini Live API).

column1: Explain: Server-sent events (SSE) and streaming responses
column2:
What: A one-way stream from server to client over a normal HTTP response (Content-Type: text/event-stream). The server keeps the response open and writes data: lines as events occur. It's simpler than WebSockets and works through most HTTP infrastructure.

How: It's the standard way LLM APIs stream tokens to clients, and it's used by MCP (streamable HTTP) and A2A for streaming updates.

What: Long polling: the client sends a request, and the server holds it until data is available or a timeout, then the client immediately re-asks. Webhooks: the provider calls *your* HTTP endpoint when something happens (a callback), for example a payment-provider status update.

How: Webhook receivers must verify authenticity (an HMAC signature header, mTLS, or an OIDC token), respond fast (queue the work and return 2xx), be idempotent (providers retry), and tolerate out-of-order delivery.

GCP: Pub/Sub push subscriptions and Eventarc are webhooks with OIDC authentication. Cloud Run is the usual receiver, often writing straight to Pub/Sub or Cloud Tasks.

column1: Explain: API design: versioning, pagination, errors, long-running operations
column2: What: Versioning: major versions in the path, additive changes within a version, deprecation policies. Pagination: prefer cursor or page tokens over offsets (stable under inserts). Errors: a consistent error model (code, message, details), as in Google's google.rpc.Status. Long-running operations: return 202 + an operation resource the client polls (or a callback), which is how Google APIs handle slow tasks. Field masks for partial updates and reads. Etags for optimistic concurrency.

What: A standard, machine-readable specification (YAML or JSON) for REST APIs: paths, operations, parameters, schemas and security schemes. It drives documentation, client and server generation, mocking, testing and gateway configuration.

GCP: API Gateway and Cloud Endpoints are configured from OpenAPI specs. Apigee imports OpenAPI to generate proxies and developer-portal docs. Agents use OpenAPI specs as tool definitions, so well-described APIs become agent tools quickly.

What: An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. Idempotency keys make non-idempotent operations safe: the client sends a unique key (for example a UUID per payment attempt), and the server stores key → result and returns the stored result for repeats instead of executing again.

How: Store keys with a TTL, atomically with the side effect (same transaction), and scope them per client. Consumers of at-least-once messages dedupe on message or business IDs.

column1: Explain: Retries, exponential backoff and jitter
column2:
What: Retrying transient failures (timeouts, 429, 503) with exponentially growing waits (for example 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms… capped) plus random jitter, so that many clients don't retry in sync and hammer a recovering service.

How: Limit attempts, and set an overall deadline. Retry only idempotent operations or those with idempotency keys. Use retry budgets (for example retries must stay under 10% of requests) to avoid retry storms.

GCP: Google client libraries retry automatically with backoff for retryable errors. Pub/Sub has retry policies. Cloud Tasks and Workflows have configurable retries.

column1: Explain: Timeouts, deadlines and deadline propagation
column2:
What: Every remote call needs a timeout. Without one, a slow dependency holds threads and connections until the caller collapses too. A deadline is an absolute "must finish by" time, propagated down the call chain so downstream services stop work the caller has already given up on.

How: Set timeouts per hop that add up to less than the user-facing budget. gRPC propagates deadlines natively.

GCP: Cloud Run request timeout, load balancer backend timeout, Apigee target timeouts, client library timeouts. LLM calls have long and variable latency, so budget for them explicitly and stream.

What: Wraps calls to a dependency. After repeated failures it opens (fails fast, without calling the dependency, maybe returning a fallback). After a cool-down it goes half-open to test with a few calls, then closes if healthy.

How: It prevents wasting resources on a dead dependency and gives the dependency room to recover.

GCP: In code (resilience libraries) or in a service mesh / Envoy (outlier detection, connection limits). Load balancer outlier detection is a related mechanism.

column1: Explain: Bulkheads, rate limiting and throttling
column2:
What: Bulkheads: isolate resources (thread pools, connection pools, instances) per dependency or tenant, so one failure can't sink the whole service. Rate limiting: cap requests per client or key in a time window. Algorithms are token bucket (allows bursts up to the bucket size), leaky bucket (smooth rate) and fixed or sliding windows. Throttling is the response: reject with 429 or delay.

GCP: Apigee (Quota, SpikeArrest policies), Cloud Armor rate-limiting rules, API Gateway quotas, Cloud Tasks queue rates, and Gemini model quotas (protect yourself from the provider's 429s too).

What: Backpressure: a slow consumer signals producers to slow down, instead of buffering until it runs out of memory (flow control in Pub/Sub StreamingPull, TCP windows, reactive streams). Load shedding: under overload, deliberately reject low-priority work early, so high-priority requests still succeed.

GCP: A queue (Pub/Sub, Cloud Tasks) between bursty producers and fragile consumers is the classic buffer. Its backlog becomes the autoscaling signal.

column1: Explain: API gateway vs API management
column2:
What: An API gateway is a reverse proxy in front of APIs that does routing, authentication, rate limiting and transformation. API management adds the full lifecycle around it: a developer portal (documentation and self-service keys), API products and plans, analytics, monetization, versioning, security policies, and governance across many teams and external consumers.

GCP: API Gateway is lightweight and serverless, for simple backends. Apigee is enterprise API management. Cloud Endpoints is legacy.

What: Google's enterprise API management platform. Very common in banks for external, partner and Open Banking APIs, and increasingly for governing access to internal APIs and AI models.

How: You define API proxies: a proxy endpoint (client-facing, "northbound") and target endpoint (backend, "southbound"), with flows of policies attached: VerifyAPIKey, OAuthV2 (Apigee as the authorization server, issuing and validating tokens), VerifyJWT, Quota, SpikeArrest, JSONThreatProtection / RegexProtection, AssignMessage (transform), ResponseCache, ServiceCallout, JavaScript or Java callouts, and shared flows (reusable policy chains, for example a corporate security flow). API products bundle proxies, scopes and quotas. Apps and developers get credentials. There's an integrated developer portal, analytics, monetization and Advanced API Security (abuse detection, security scoring). Deployment models: Apigee X (Google-managed; networking northbound through an external or internal load balancer, or PSC, and southbound to backends through PSC or VPC peering) and Apigee hybrid (you run the runtime plane on your own Kubernetes on-prem or in another cloud, while Google hosts the management plane).

GCP: Apigee as an AI gateway: proxies in front of model endpoints (Gemini, Claude through Model Garden, internal models) enforce authentication, token-based quotas per team, PII checks (calling Sensitive Data Protection or Model Armor), logging, semantic caching and model routing, giving one governed front door for every LLM call in the bank. Check current Apigee docs for the latest LLM-specific policies.

column1: Explain: API Gateway and Cloud Endpoints
column2: What: API Gateway: a fully managed gateway configured from an OpenAPI spec, for Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions and App Engine backends, with API keys, JWT validation and quotas. Cheaper and simpler than Apigee, but without a portal, monetization or rich policies. Cloud Endpoints: the older option based on the Extensible Service Proxy (ESPv2/Envoy) sidecar.

What: How a service finds the current network location of another. DNS-based (Kubernetes Service DNS names, Cloud DNS private zones), registry-based (Service Directory, Consul), or handled by the mesh.

GCP: Cloud Run services have stable URLs (discovery is easy). In GKE, use service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Service Directory registers endpoints across GKE, VMs and on-prem.

What: A monolith deploys as one unit: simple to build, test and run; it scales as a whole, and coordinating releases gets harder as teams grow. Microservices are independently deployable services around business capabilities, each owning its data: they allow independent scaling and release, at the cost of distributed-systems complexity (network failures, eventual consistency, observability, many deployments).

How: A modular monolith is often the right first step. Split out services where independent scaling, team autonomy or different release cadences pay for the complexity.

What: Orchestration: a central coordinator tells each service what to do and tracks the overall state (for example Workflows, Composer, an agent orchestrator). It's easy to see and change the flow, but the coordinator becomes coupled to everything. Choreography: services react to each other's events with no central controller. It's loosely coupled, but the end-to-end flow is implicit and harder to trace.

GCP: Orchestration: Workflows, Cloud Composer, Cloud Tasks chains, ADK workflow agents. Choreography: Pub/Sub and Eventarc.

What: Keeping data consistent across services *without* a distributed ACID transaction. A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails (reserve funds → book FX → transfer; if the transfer fails, release the FX booking, then release the funds).

How: It can be orchestrated (a coordinator such as Workflows) or choreographed (events). Every step and compensation must be idempotent.

What: Solves the "dual write" problem: updating your database *and* publishing an event can't be atomic across two systems. Instead, write the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change. A separate relay (a poller, or CDC) publishes outbox rows to Pub/Sub or Kafka.

GCP: Cloud SQL or AlloyDB outbox + a Datastream or Debezium relay, or Spanner change streams → Dataflow → Pub/Sub.

What: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) uses separate models for writes and reads (for example writes to Spanner, reads from a denormalized BigQuery or Elasticsearch view). Event sourcing stores state as an append-only log of events and derives current state by replaying them. That gives a full audit history, which suits ledgers, but adds complexity.

What: GCP's event routing service. It delivers events in the CloudEvents format from sources to targets.

How: Sources: direct events (Cloud Storage object finalized, Pub/Sub messages, Firestore changes, and more), Cloud Audit Logs events (almost any API call on GCP, for example "a BigQuery table was created"), and third-party providers. Targets: Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions, GKE services, Workflows, internal HTTP endpoints. Triggers have filters, and run as a service account that needs invoker rights. Eventarc Advanced adds a central message bus with routing, filtering and transformation across many publishers and subscribers.

GCP: "When a document lands in this bucket, start the RAG ingestion job" is a one-trigger Eventarc pattern.
What: A CNCF specification for describing events in a common way (id, source, type, time, subject, data), so producers and consumers across platforms interoperate.

What: Managed queues of HTTP (or App Engine) tasks, where each task is a request to a *specific* target. You get explicit control: rate limits (dispatches per second, max concurrent), retries with backoff, scheduled delivery (run at time X), and deduplication by task name.

GCP: Use it to protect a fragile downstream (a legacy core banking API that can take only 50 requests per second), or for deferred work per user. Pub/Sub is better for fan-out and decoupled events, where the publisher doesn't know the consumers.
What: A managed cron service. It triggers HTTP targets (with OIDC or OAuth authentication), Pub/Sub topics or App Engine on a schedule, with retries.

What: Serverless orchestration of services and APIs, defined in YAML or JSON: steps, conditions, loops, parallel branches, variables, try/retry/except error handling, connectors for Google APIs (with long-running operations handled for you), callbacks (wait for external events or human approval), and executions that can last up to a year.

GCP: Good for sagas, document-processing pipelines, approval flows ("generate a credit memo with Gemini → wait for underwriter approval via callback → file it"), and gluing Cloud Run services together without writing orchestration code.

column1: Explain: Application Integration and Integration Connectors
column2: What: Google's iPaaS: low-code integration flows with Integration Connectors to SaaS and enterprise systems (Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, databases, mainframes and so on). The connectors can also be exposed as tools for AI agents.

What: How data is encoded on the wire or on disk. JSON (human-readable, flexible, verbose), Protocol Buffers (binary, schema'd, compact, the RPC standard), Avro (binary, schema travels with the data, common in Kafka and Pub/Sub schemas), Parquet / ORC (columnar files for analytics, used in data lakes and BigLake), CSV (simple, fragile).

What: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: the browser rule that blocks a web page on origin A from reading responses from API origin B, unless B returns headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin and others) allowing it. Non-simple requests trigger a preflight OPTIONS request.

What: Availability = the proportion of time (or of requests) a service works. Downtime budgets: 99% ≈ 7.3 h/month · 99.9% ≈ 43.8 min/month · 99.95% ≈ 21.9 min/month · 99.99% ≈ 4.4 min/month · 99.999% ≈ 26 s/month.

How: Serial dependencies multiply: a service that needs A (99.95%) *and* B (99.95%) is at most about 99.9%. Redundancy improves availability: two independent 99% replicas, where either can serve, give about 99.99%.

column1: Explain: SLI, SLO, SLA and error budgets
column2:
What: SLI (indicator): a measured ratio of good events to total events, for example the proportion of requests that return 2xx within 300 ms. SLO (objective): the internal target for an SLI over a window, for example 99.9% over 28 days. SLA (agreement): a contractual promise with penalties, set looser than the SLO. Error budget: 100% − SLO, the amount of unreliability you're allowed to "spend" on releases, experiments and incidents.

How: An error budget policy says what happens when the budget is used up: freeze features and focus on reliability. That's what makes SLOs drive decisions rather than sit on dashboards.

GCP: Cloud Monitoring SLO monitoring (request-based or windows-based SLIs on Cloud Run, GKE, load balancers, Cloud Service Mesh or custom metrics) with burn-rate alerts. Google publishes SLAs per product (for example Cloud Run 99.95%, Spanner multi-region 99.999%). Your SLO can't be higher than your dependencies allow.

What: Alerting on *how fast* you're consuming the error budget instead of on raw thresholds. A burn rate of 1 uses exactly the budget over the window. 14.4× over 1 hour means 2% of a 30-day budget gone in an hour, which should page someone.

How: Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts (a fast window for sudden outages, a slow one for gradual degradation). This gives high precision (few false pages) and good recall.

column1: Explain: High availability vs disaster recovery
column2: What: High availability (HA): survive *component and zone* failures automatically with little or no disruption (redundancy within a region). Disaster recovery (DR): recover from *large-scale* events (region loss, data corruption, ransomware, a cyber attack) to a defined RTO and RPO, often involving a failover decision.

What: RTO (Recovery Time Objective): the maximum acceptable time to restore service. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time (for example "the last 5 minutes of transactions").

How: RPO drives the replication and backup design (synchronous → RPO ≈ 0; async → seconds to minutes; nightly backup → up to 24 h). RTO drives the standby design (hot, warm, cold) and the level of automation.

column1: Explain: DR patterns: backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active
column2:
What: Backup and restore (cold): only backups in another region; rebuild on disaster (RTO hours or days, cheapest). Pilot light: core data replicated and minimal infrastructure defined (often as code), scaled up on failover. Warm standby: a scaled-down but running copy in region 2, with replicated databases (RTO minutes). Hot / active-active: full capacity in multiple regions serving traffic simultaneously (global load balancing + multi-region databases; RTO ≈ 0; most expensive and complex).

GCP: IaC (Terraform) + cross-region Cloud SQL or AlloyDB replicas + a dual- or multi-region GCS bucket + Artifact Registry in multiple regions + a global load balancer gives a typical warm standby. Spanner multi-region + global load balancing + Cloud Run in two or more regions gives active-active. Rehearse it: a DR plan that hasn't been tested doesn't count.

column1: Explain: Failure domains: zones and regions
column2:
What: A failure domain is a set of resources that can fail together. In GCP, a zone is a failure domain within a region (independent power, cooling and networking). A region is a geographic area of three or more zones.

How: Zonal resources (VMs, zonal disks) need multi-zone redundancy for HA. Regional resources (regional MIGs, Cloud Run, Cloud SQL HA, regional Spanner) handle zone failure for you. Multi-region resources handle region failure. Check each product's documented failure behaviour.

GCP: London is europe-west2 (3 zones), and it's currently Google Cloud's only UK region. UK banks therefore usually get HA from multiple London zones. For region-level DR they pair it with another region (often europe-west1, Belgium) where data policy allows data to leave the UK, or with on-prem. Check current region availability and your bank's residency policy.

What: Provisioning enough spare capacity that losing one unit (an instance, a zone) still leaves enough to serve peak load. With 3 zones, each zone must handle 50% of peak if one fails (N+1 across zones). For maintenance during an outage you need N+2.

What: Keeping core functions working when parts fail: serve cached balances if the live ledger is slow, disable recommendations rather than the whole app, fall back to a smaller model or a "please try later" response when the LLM provider returns 429s.

What: Monitoring watches known signals and alerts on known failure modes (dashboards, thresholds). Observability is the ability to understand *new, unexpected* behaviour from the telemetry the system emits: logs (discrete events), metrics (numeric time series), traces (request paths across services), plus profiles.

GCP: Google Cloud Observability: Cloud Logging, Cloud Monitoring, Cloud Trace, Cloud Profiler, Error Reporting, Managed Service for Prometheus. All of it is OpenTelemetry-friendly.

What: Collects, stores, searches and routes logs from GCP services, your apps (stdout/stderr on Cloud Run and GKE, the Ops Agent on VMs) and audit logs.

How: The Log Router checks every entry against sinks (include and exclusion filters) → destinations: log buckets (with configurable retention and region, CMEK, and optional Log Analytics for SQL queries), BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, or other projects. The _Required bucket (audit and admin logs, 400 days, unchangeable) and the _Default bucket (30 days, configurable) exist in every project. Query with the Logging query language in Logs Explorer. Log-based metrics turn matching entries into counters or distributions.

column1: Explain: Structured logging and log correlation
column2:
What: Writing logs as JSON with fields (severity, message, request ID, user ID, logging.googleapis.com/trace) instead of free text, so they're queryable and correlated.

GCP: On Cloud Run and GKE, JSON lines on stdout are parsed automatically. Include the trace ID so the Logs Explorer can show every log line for one request alongside its trace.

What: Metrics, dashboards and alerting for GCP, hybrid and multicloud resources.

How: Built-in metrics for every service (no setup), custom metrics (OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, the API), log-based metrics, Metrics Explorer, PromQL querying, dashboards (including multi-project with metrics scopes), alerting policies (metric thresholds, absence, log-match, SLO burn-rate) → notification channels (email, SMS, Slack, PagerDuty, webhooks, Pub/Sub), uptime checks and synthetic monitors (scripted probes of user journeys), Personalized Service Health (Google-side incidents affecting your projects).

GCP: A metrics scope lets one project view metrics from many, which is how a central SRE or SOC team sees the whole estate.

What: Following one request across services. A trace is a tree of spans (timed operations with attributes). Context propagation passes the trace ID and span ID in headers (W3C traceparent) from hop to hop.

How: The waterfall view shows where latency goes ("80% of this request was the LLM call; 15% was vector search").

GCP: Cloud Trace (with OpenTelemetry), with automatic spans for load balancers, Cloud Run and many client libraries. For agents, tracing is essential: each model call, tool call and retrieval should be a span. ADK and Agent Runtime emit traces.

What: The vendor-neutral CNCF standard and SDKs for generating and exporting traces, metrics and logs (with semantic conventions, now including GenAI conventions for model calls and token usage), plus the OpenTelemetry Collector for processing and routing.

GCP: Google Cloud Observability ingests OTLP natively. Instrumenting once with OTel avoids lock-in to any observability backend.

column1: Explain: Golden signals, RED and USE
column2:
What: Frameworks for choosing what to measure. Four golden signals (Google SRE): latency, traffic, errors, saturation. RED (for services): Rate, Errors, Duration. USE (for resources): Utilization, Saturation, Errors.

How: Alert on user-facing symptoms (golden signals and SLO burn), and use resource metrics (USE) for diagnosis and capacity.

What: Good alerts are actionable (a human must do something), symptom-based (users are affected) and urgent-only for pages. Everything else becomes a ticket or a dashboard. Each alert links a playbook / runbook.

What: A structured response: detect → declare → assign roles (incident commander, communications lead, operations) → mitigate first (roll back, fail over, shed load) → resolve → blameless postmortem (timeline, root and contributing causes, action items with owners).
What: SRE term for manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales with the service and has no lasting value. SRE practice caps toil (for example at 50% of time) and automates the rest.

column1: Explain: Quotas, limits and capacity planning
column2: What: Quotas cap how much of a resource a project can use. Rate quotas limit API calls per minute (including Gemini requests and tokens per minute). Allocation quotas limit the count of resources (CPUs per region, IP addresses). They can usually be raised through a request. System limits are hard ceilings. Capacity planning forecasts demand and ensures headroom: quota increases, reservations (guaranteed VM or GPU capacity in a zone), committed use discounts, and Provisioned Throughput for models.

column1: Explain: Load testing and chaos engineering
column2:
What: Load testing: generate realistic traffic to find capacity limits and bottlenecks before users do (Locust, k6, JMeter; distributed on GKE). Chaos engineering: deliberately inject failures (kill instances, add latency, fail a zone or dependency) in a controlled way, to verify that resilience mechanisms actually work.

GCP: Fault injection in the load balancer or service mesh, stopping zones in DR tests, failing over Cloud SQL deliberately. It aligns with the operational resilience requirement to test against severe but plausible scenarios.

What: Recreate: stop the old, start the new (downtime). Rolling: replace instances gradually. Blue/green: run the new version alongside the old, switch all traffic at once, keep blue for instant rollback. Canary: send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watch the metrics, then increase. A/B testing: split by user segment to compare behaviour. Shadow / mirroring: send a copy of real traffic to the new version without returning its responses. Feature flags: deploy code dark and toggle behaviour at runtime, which separates *deploy* from *release*.

GCP: Cloud Run revisions + traffic splitting + tags. GKE through Deployments, the Gateway API and Cloud Deploy canaries. MIG rolling updates. Load balancer weighted backends and traffic mirroring.

What: Continuous Integration: every change is merged frequently and automatically built and tested (unit tests, linters, SAST, dependency and container scanning). Continuous Delivery: every change is *releasable*, promoted through environments by an automated pipeline, often with approval gates. Continuous Deployment: every passing change goes to production automatically. This all sits inside the SDLC (software development life cycle): plan → design → build → test → release → operate, with security built into every stage ("shift left").

GCP: Source (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Secure Source Manager) → Cloud Build (CI) → Artifact Registry (images + SBOM + provenance) → Binary Authorization → Cloud Deploy (CD across dev → test → prod targets, with approvals and canaries) → GKE or Cloud Run. Or GitHub Actions authenticating with Workload Identity Federation.

What: Build-time secrets are needed to *build* (for example a token for a private package registry). Use them in the build step only, from Secret Manager, and never let them end up in image layers. Runtime secrets are needed by the running app (database passwords, API keys). Inject them at deploy or run time (Cloud Run or GKE secret mounts, Secret Manager API) so the same image works in every environment and rotation doesn't need a rebuild.

What: Serverless CI. Builds run as a series of steps (each a container) defined in cloudbuild.yaml, triggered by git events, Pub/Sub, webhooks or manually. It produces images and artifacts with SLSA provenance.

How: Runs as a configurable service account (least privilege). Private pools run builds inside your VPC with no public internet access, required by many banks to reach private repositories and artifact proxies.

What: Managed continuous delivery to GKE, Cloud Run and GKE-attached clusters. You define a delivery pipeline of ordered targets (environments). Releases are promoted through them with approvals, automated or manual canary and blue/green strategies, verification jobs, rollbacks, and full audit history. It uses Skaffold for rendering and deploying.

What: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled code instead of console clicks. You get repeatability, code review, audit trail, drift detection and rebuild-from-scratch DR.

How: Declarative tools (Terraform, Config Connector) describe the desired end state, and the tool works out the changes (plan) and applies them. Imperative scripts (gcloud) describe steps.

GCP: Terraform (the industry default, with the google provider), Infrastructure Manager (Google-managed Terraform runs, state and history), Config Connector (GCP resources as Kubernetes custom resources), Cloud Foundation Fabric / FAST (opinionated modules and a staged enterprise org bootstrap) and the Cloud Foundation Toolkit.

column1: Explain: Terraform state, plan and drift
column2: What: State is Terraform's record mapping code to real resources. Keep it in a remote backend (a GCS bucket with versioning; locking prevents concurrent applies). Plan shows the diff before apply. Drift happens when someone changes resources outside Terraform.

What: Git is the single source of truth for desired state. An agent in the cluster (Config Sync, Argo CD, Flux) continuously pulls and reconciles, so changes happen only through reviewed pull requests, and drift is corrected automatically.

column1: Explain: Immutable infrastructure and configuration management
column2: What: Instead of patching running servers in place, build a new image or container and replace the instances. This removes configuration drift and makes rollback trivial. Configuration is injected at deploy time (env vars, Secret Manager, ConfigMaps), never baked per environment into the image.

What: Separate dev → test/UAT → pre-prod → prod environments, usually separate projects (or folders), each with its own IAM, network and data. The *same artifact* (image digest) is promoted through them. In banks, prod data generally can't be used in lower environments without masking or synthetic replacement. Ephemeral environments (spun up per pull request from IaC, then destroyed) give realistic testing without permanent cost.

What: Unit (functions in isolation), integration (with real or emulated dependencies; GCP has emulators for Pub/Sub, Firestore, Bigtable, Spanner and Datastore, run through gcloud emulators or Cloud Code in the IDE), contract (consumer and provider API expectations), end-to-end, performance / load, security (SAST, DAST, dependency scanning, pen tests), DR tests. Evaluation suites for LLM and agent behaviour are an AI-specific addition.

What: Machine-learning-driven recommendations across GCP: idle VMs, disks and IPs, VM rightsizing, committed-use purchases, IAM excess permissions, unattended projects, and network and security improvements. They're available through the console, API and the BigQuery export.

What: An AI assistant in the Google Cloud console that helps design architectures, explain resources and costs, troubleshoot (investigations that analyze logs, metrics and configuration) and generate configurations. It appears in the newer exam guides. It's useful, but always verify its suggestions.

column1: Explain: App Hub and Cloud Hub
column2: What: App Hub groups resources across projects into *applications* (services and workloads with owners, criticality and environment attributes), so monitoring, cost and governance can be organised by application rather than by project. Cloud Hub is a console home that shows application health, active incidents, deployments, quotas and other operational signals in one place. Both appear in the newer exam guides.

What: Organization (root, tied to a Cloud Identity / Workspace domain) → Folders (nestable, typically by business unit, environment or both) → Projects (the unit of billing, API enablement, quotas and most IAM) → Resources.

How: IAM policies, org policies, tags and some firewall policies inherit downwards. A project has an immutable, globally unique project ID, a mutable name and a Google-assigned number. Deleting a project shuts it down, and it can be restored within 30 days.

GCP: Bank layouts usually look like org → {common/shared, prod, non-prod, sandbox} → business-unit folders → app/env projects. Each design choice there changes which policies are easiest to apply.

column1: Explain: Landing zone and enterprise foundations
column2:
What: The pre-built, governed foundation that workloads land in: identity integration, hierarchy, org policies, networking (Shared VPC hubs, hybrid connectivity, DNS), centralized logging and monitoring, security tooling (SCC, KMS), billing setup, and a project factory (automated, compliant project creation).

GCP: Google's enterprise foundations blueprint and Cloud Foundation Fabric FAST are the reference implementations, deployed with Terraform. In a bank, the platform team owns it, and you mostly consume it, but you need to understand it to design within it.

What: How workloads are split into projects. Common practice: one project per application per environment (for example payments-api-dev / -prod), plus shared projects (network host, logging, security, CI/CD, shared data).

How: Projects are free. They give isolation of IAM, quotas, billing and blast radius. Too few means shared permissions and noisy neighbours. Too many needs automation (a project factory) and consistent naming and labels.

What: Key/value metadata on most resources (env=prod, team=fraud, cost-centre=1234, data-class=confidential), used for filtering, automation and cost allocation (labels appear in billing exports). Labels have no security effect.

What: A searchable inventory of all resources and IAM policies across the org, with a history of changes (about 35 days), real-time feeds to Pub/Sub, and exports to BigQuery for analysis ("every bucket without CMEK", "every service account with Owner").

What: Per-project or per-region caps on resources (CPUs, IPs, GPUs) and API rates (requests per minute, tokens per minute). They protect both Google's capacity and you (from runaway spend or a bug). Most can be increased by request. Quota adjuster can automate increases. You can also *lower* quotas yourself as a cost guardrail (for example capping BigQuery bytes scanned per day).

column1: Explain: Billing accounts and billing structure
column2:
What: A Cloud Billing account pays for one or more linked projects. It can be self-serve (card) or invoiced. Subaccounts are for resellers. Billing IAM roles are separate from project roles (Billing Account Administrator, User, Viewer).

How: Unlinking billing stops paid services in the project. Only principals with Billing Account User on the account can link projects to it.
What: Thresholds on actual or forecasted spend for a billing account, filtered by projects, services or labels, that notify by email or publish to Pub/Sub (for automated responses).

column1: Explain: Billing export to BigQuery and FinOps reporting
